in writing. by establishing a single application procedure for third-country nationals wishing to be admitted to the territory of a member state to work there and by offering them a secure legal status, this proposal for a directive will simplify the often complex administrative procedures for the reception of economic migrants. the existence of a single procedure for issuing a single document authorising residence and access to the labour market constitutes a significant simplification of the admission system. the proposal also provides for equal treatment with national workers and therefore has the advantage of giving workers from third countries greater protection than at present. this status will also help to combat unfair competition which often results from the absence of a legal status protecting these workers. the text adopted today also takes up the two main priorities of the adle: it removes all reference to additional documents and asks the member states to draw up 'matching tables' which enable the commission to verify the transposition of the directive. it thus gives a clear signal of the european parliament's willingness to move towards a european legislative framework for legal immigration.
in writing. the adoption this afternoon of the directive on a single permit for third-country nationals wishing to reside and work in a member state is a further step towards achieving a harmonised immigration policy at european level. the idea of merging a residence permit and a work permit is a good one. it shows that the union is genuinely committed to promoting legal migration and that it is not the fortress europe that some want to see in it. to do this it was important that the european parliament supported the idea of a single application procedure which would be simpler and faster for both the employer and the migrant. the european parliament also made the right choice by excluding from the scope of application four categories of workers: seasonal workers, workers posted within their undertakings, self-employed persons and seamen, already or soon to be covered by specific directives. another positive aspect is the flexibility which member states have in respect of the actual rights of third country workers. the 27 capitals have the final say on whether or not to grant unemployment benefits and family allowances and whether or not to grant social housing during the first three years of residence. just common sense!
in writing. - although the directive is far from ideal and complete, i voted in favour of the directive on a single procedure for applying for a residence and work permit. i regret the shortcomings in relation to seasonal workers, posted workers, the right to change employers and the right to enter and re-enter, because these subgroups are protected in other (future) regulations. all in all, this directive is of great importance as it is the first of its kind to provide a common package of minimum rights (including wage rights, equal treatment in the workplace, pension rights, access to health care) to third country workers legally resident in europe, on the basis of equal treatment with national workers of the member states. in addition, a simplified system with a single application procedure for a residence and work permit is provided for. this is far from a fully common immigration policy, but in view of the growing immigration flows, the constantly changing demand for foreign labour and the prevention of abuse and discrimination in this respect, this initial protection is essential. third country workers will now be given more protection than they are at present. all of that was the deciding factor in my yes vote.
in writing. - the facilitation of crossborder trade through uniform rules and at the same time the strengthening of consumer rights, especially when buying in another member state, are the reasons why i expressly welcome the 'new' consumer protection directive. the current uncertainty about the applicable consumer rights is deterring both companies from offering their goods cross-border and consumers from ordering these goods, as there is uncertainty about a possible withdrawal. a european single market explicitly calls for the removal of such barriers. the uniform definitions proposed in this report, which harmonise, inter alia, the right of withdrawal and rules on abusive contractual terms, will create legal certainty and thus increase the attractiveness of crossborder trade for businesses and thus ultimately benefit consumers. chapter 5 was not adopted, so consumer protection in europe will apply across europe according to the highest criteria. referral to the committee is therefore necessary to renegotiate with the commission.
in writing. a well-protected consumer is a secure citizen and a sign of the maturity of our modern democracies. this is where the directive adopted today is important. not a day goes by without the european consumer, when making a purchase online or accepting a modification to a telephone subscription contract, being confronted with a question about the conformity of the signed or approved contract. it is in response to the often unbalanced relations between traders and consumers that the european parliament has opted for a 14-day right of withdrawal. a clear signal that the same rights should be exercised throughout the union. so of course the adoption of the schwab report does not fully satisfy either the consumer associations opposed to the principle of maximum harmonisation or the representatives of smes and chambers of commerce who wanted the legislation to be limited to boosting e-commerce. the european parliament has chosen the compromise and has not given in to the sirens of alarm. this choice is supported by the recent european survey which shows that 79% of the traders surveyed believe that the legislation adopted will have little impact on their sales abroad.

madam president, mr van rompuy, it is clear that there are obvious things in your conclusions that we cannot be against: rigorous governance. no one can argue with that. but rigor should not mean zero deficit or austerity, but rather smart spending. the necessary competitiveness of the union must be improved, that is obvious, but the only adjustment variable cannot be lower wages or cuts in social spending. competitiveness is achieved through investment in skills, research, excellence and large-scale infrastructure. everyone here agrees that the union and the euro are at a turning point. we must choose between a model of withdrawal into ourselves, in which each one looks at his competitiveness in relation to the neighbouring member state, his rating on the financial markets, his lowest possible contribution to the european budget, or choose a model of solidarity - the only acceptable one - in which social standards are raised, in particular by respecting the place of social dialogue and trade unions, with social minimums throughout europe and mechanisms for indexing salaries, in which solidarity between the generations is ensured by a pension system that guarantees an adequate level of living in dignity, as parliament recently said. the member states should be freed from the pressures of the financial markets by means of a european central bank with a strengthened role and better regulated rating agencies, a model of solidarity which ensures genuine social and territorial cohesion in europe, in particular through a strengthened european budget, with a thorough reform of its own resources, and finally the introduction of the financial transaction tax. your conclusions are based on a strong ideology in which debt and deficits are the cause of the crisis, while the real cause is the irresponsibility of financial actors. without a change of ideological perspective within the council, we shall not get out of the crisis, we shall not restore the citizens' confidence. there is a clear democratic deficit today and if the council and the commission continue to make proposals which do not take parliament's opinion into account, the rejection of our project by our fellow citizens will intensify a little more.
the past year has been a year of hard work and many reforms have been put in place to ensure that the union will continue to be a society in which people live and work in a good and just way. i therefore welcome the fact that the european council has been given a new mandate. after all that has been said by the members, i would like to make three points. my first one concerns wage costs as one of the factors in competition policy. during the crisis i have heard the president of the commission and the president of the european council speak in praise of automatic stabilisers on several occasions. instead of sharp peaks and troughs, they make for a more stable economy with less job loss, which fits perfectly into the social market economy we want to be. but some now fear that too strong a focus on factor wage costs in the euro plus pact would severely restrict the scope for these automatic stabilisers. my question is, mr president, how do you see this? a second consideration is the wage cost factor. i hear the trade unions constantly saying that the autonomy of the member states and their social partners would be undermined in the area of wage formation and that we might be aiming at a flagrant breach of the rules of competence of the treaty. my question is: are we really in a danger zone there or is that fear unfounded? i would also like to hear your analysis, mr president-in-office, because if this double fear is unjustified, then we really must help to eliminate it. finally, a question on the common consolidated corporate tax base. i read one sentence in the conclusions of the spring summit, barely one, and yet without the slightest commitment from the european council on the matter. i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to give us a clear answer to this question. thank you in advance for your answers.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the council conclusions on economic policy and the euro-plus pact open up a veritable european pandora's box, from which nothing but ills emerge that the european citizens will have to face. the challenge to social protection and wage indexation, the link between productivity and wages, the fall in purchasing power, the increase in the retirement age are just a few examples of the austerity crisis that awaits us. i am appalled to see that the council has clearly failed to learn the lessons of the crisis. of course we need a policy of fiscal responsibility and rigour, no one disputes this, but we must not put all the burden on the citizens, who represent our only chance of being able to get out of this crisis from above. you are too quick to forget the financial and banking sector, which must also bear the necessary burden and, above all, take responsibility. when will we finally see a financial transaction tax? the council is putting the burden of the sacrifices on labour and workers, not on capital, at a time when 16 million europeans are unemployed, prices are soaring and speculative shocks are shaking the continent, and this is unacceptable.
president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as regards the evaluation of the last european council, i think that the analysis i presented was fairly balanced, fairly reasonable. i think it's fair to say that we've made some very significant progress on the structure. if we compare what we have now with what we did not have before, it is surely a great improvement. for example, there was the creation of a permanent stability mechanism, which was not even provided for in the treaty. in fact, this parliament, by an overwhelming majority, supported a limited reform of the treaty to create a new instrument, an instrument which did not even exist before. so let's be intellectually honest in our evaluation. i think there has been significant progress in terms of responding to the crisis, in terms of learning from the shortcomings we have seen in the past, both in terms of instruments and policies. but at the same time, i said, very clearly, that it might not be enough. it's one thing to have the structure, the architecture, but it's another thing to have the policies to enforce. and indeed, the real test of success is to see, after that, what governments, and also our institutions, can do in terms of substance. the substance is more important than the instruments. but at the same time i have told you, with, i think, great transparency, that when we talk about ambition, the commission would have preferred to go further in certain areas. we have stressed, for example, that we are in favour of more flexibility for the permanent stability mechanism. unfortunately, consensus at this higher level of ambition was not possible. that said, i think it would be a mistake to dismiss the gains we have made. i would like to emphasize this important aspect of ambition, because some have suggested that the commission should make other proposals. virtually everything you have said has already been proposed by the commission. on 9 may 2010, the commission myself and commissioner rehn tabled a legislative proposal for a fully community approach in terms of the stability mechanism. we have proposed the pooling of debt management, for example, in what is known as joint and several guarantees. this has been refused by our member states. not by you, but the member states are essential, mr verhofstadt. we presented the text at the euro summit. this was insisted in the presence of the president of the european council, with some heads of state and government, that they accept a qualified majority rule. it was denied! so we can always insist, but the in writing. what if the farmer is the future of the common agricultural policy? this statement is somewhat provocative, but it is largely justified when one refers to the importance of the female population in rural life and on the farm. statistics show that in the european union, women farmers represent 43% of the agricultural workforce and 20% of women are farm managers, not to mention spouses whose work is often not recorded. in the age of specialisation of farms, the creative spirit of women is an undeniable plus which, coupled with their greater concern for a sustainable and quality environment, deserves to be recognised and supported at european level. this is the choice made this afternoon by the european parliament, which, in adopting the jeggle report, underlined the importance that women will play in the future in the revaluation of the rural environment. as the rapporteur rightly says in the explanatory statement: 'experience shows that the quality of life and economic power depend, mainly in rural areas, on the presence and commitment of women'. a simple, modern way of looking at farming in a new way.
in writing. i am pleased with the adoption of mrs jeggle's report, in which i was personally involved. the cap has a social value in recognising the fundamental role of women in preserving the future prospects of life and prosperity in rural areas (considering that 41% of the 14.6 million people employed in agriculture in the european union are women). these include promoting women's entrepreneurship and skills in agriculture, equipping rural areas with modern infrastructure to enable them to reconcile work and family life (through the creation of crèches, for example), aiming for greater representation of women in the political, economic and social bodies of the agricultural sector (with a clear aim of absolute parity), establishing adequate social security for women working in agriculture and ensuring shared ownership of agricultural holdings. if 'the first equality is equity', the recognition of the role of women in agriculture is taking on a new dimension.

for the greens/efa group madam president, i would like to continue by reacting to a number of things that have been said and i will start with what catherine trautmann said. we are told - and it is true - that the radio spectrum is a scarce commodity. i would first like to emphasize that this is a matter of common interest. it is a good which no one can claim as his exclusive property. so, for us, no actor whatsoever can claim to have some sort of pre-emptive right, acquired right, over the spectrum, and i think that's something that's established by this relationship. if it is a common and rare commodity, it is useful, on the one hand, to understand the use made of it today. hence the idea of a broad and comprehensive examination of the current use of spectrum by all actors, including those just mentioned by mr giles, namely, for example, the civil security services and even the military. it is really important to understand what the real use of this scarce resource is today because, in our opinion, it is far from optimal. on the other hand, it is a question of having a transparent process for allocating this rare property, but also sufficiently dynamic, to avoid the creation of new logics of acquired rights. i would also like to draw attention to the principles of allocation and auctioning of spectrum because indeed, not all uses are necessarily commercial in nature and therefore do not necessarily generate profits. i am thinking of course of the cultural dimension, as has been emphasized, but also of the use of public services - let us speak of civil security services - and even of military use. if we apply exclusively a market logic, we obviously run the risk of giving priority - or, at any rate, exaggerated rights - to market players whose size is known to create market distortions, in other words, small players do not always have the opportunity to compete with them. finally, i would like to draw attention to the fact that the exponential use of the radio spectrum also has implications for public health. i know that is not the subject of the report, but i think we will have to keep a very close eye on this because our citizens are worried.

in writing. by adopting mrs fraga estévez's report this afternoon, parliament gave its approval to the conclusion by the european union of a binding international agreement to combat illegal fishing, thus demonstrating its commitment to responsible fishing. it should be recalled that illegal fishing remains one of the greatest threats to the sustainable exploitation of marine biological resources and is as much a scourge as intensive fishing. countering this fishing practice, which undermines marine biological resources and marine ecosystems, is a key objective for the european union. the recent announcement by commissioner maria damanaki of a new fisheries control system ensuring the traceability of fish from the place of capture to the plate is encouraging. i note in particular the introduction on 1 january 2012 of a new points system (up to the withdrawal of the licence) which aims to ensure the uniform treatment of serious infringements, with deterrent fines of at least five times the market value of illegally caught fish. this traceability system, together with the powers of control and sanction given to inspectors posted throughout europe, is an indispensable tool in combating illegal fishing.

in writing. - mr president, i voted in favour of mr itälä's report, but i have a reservation on paragraph 113. i am totally opposed to this paragraph, which proposes a new interpretation procedure for the 'working groups'. i cannot agree with it because the proposed system: - is not compatible with the principle of equal treatment of the official languages of the union and of their users; - in the long run undoubtedly leads to the exclusion of languages other than the six mentioned; - it is impossible to organise it in a workable way, simply because the request for a supplementary language may have to be submitted before the member knows the agenda of the sitting; - makes language policy a power game. if we really want to cut back on language issues, we must demand equal efforts from everyone. and if it is no longer considered important for some members to be able to use their language, it is no longer important for other members either. there is therefore only one alternative if the interpreting work in the "working groups" is to be cut back: active and passive use of english and english only. in that case, everyone is equal before the law and there's real cutbacks.

on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, let us be very open and blunt about this: what we have seen in recent weeks on this issue has been shameful – italy issuing temporary residence permits to refugees from tunisia, then france reacting by reintroducing internal border checks, as if the european union had suddenly ceased to exist. let us be very open and call this by its name: it was a ping-pong game by two governments, and by berlusconi and sarkozy, on the back of refugees who are, in fact, in trouble. that is what has been happening and, in my opinion, it has been disastrous not only for schengen but also for the european union and its image because the reintroduction of internal border checks contradicts the whole essence of the union and the basic principles of the treaty. that point has been made several times here and mr barroso has also made it. moreover, what occurred was absolutely out of proportion. i would not go so far as to echo mr schulz in calling this a marginal problem – 27 000 tunisians do not constitute a marginal problem – but he is right to say that, by comparison with, for example, the 350 000 people who fled from kosovo during the kosovo war, we are clearly not talking about a migration tsunami. and so we come to the problem: the communication from the commission. in my opinion, it was not very clear. the communication states that, as a last resort in truly critical situations, a mechanism may need to be introduced – and, as i read it, that means a new mechanism – allowing for a coordinated and temporary reintroduction of controls. that is the problem with the whole communication because, if this means that the commission is proposing an additional possibility for the reintroduction of border controls, not provided for in the existing schengen acquis, i can tell you that our group will fight such a proposal with all available means, and i hope the entire parliament will do likewise. if, on the contrary, the sentence in question means that the commission wants to restrict the current provision, then that has been foreseen: national security and public order are the two elements covered by the existing schengen acquis. if the intended meaning is that the commission wants to restrict the current provision allowing member states to reintroduce border controls, then, mr barroso, you can have 100% support from our group. so, what i am asking of ms malmström and mr barroso is a rewriting of the communication and specifically of the sentence which states that a new mechanism shall be introduced for the reintroduction of border checks. all they need to do is to state that they will strengthen the existing provision in the schengen acquis.
president, schengen provides that checks at the internal borders of the eu are abolished, but that the external borders are checked. the problem is that the agreement is not being respected, because the external borders are not being controlled effectively. so we must dare to admit that 16 years after the schengen was established, the treaty has not been a success. we must also dare to admit that the eu is not the solution but has become part of the problem. the member states must therefore be given the opportunity to protect their borders without eu interference. more measures are urgently needed. for example, frontex should send back boats with fake refugees to their countries of origin instead of playing some kind of refined reception committee. the networks of traffickers must be dealt with very harshly. member states should stop rewarding illegal aliens with residence permits. illegal and rejected political refugees must be effectively returned. if all that does not happen, i can guarantee you that schengen is finished and that would not be a bad thing. i would also like to protest, mr president, against the use of words here, against abusive terms such as populist, extremist, etc. for people who simply want to protect the borders of their country. this has to stop. this is not correct. we also have to admit that the rules have to be applied; but we are not talking about applying the rules, we are just beginning to scold.
member of the commission. − madam president, this has been a very interesting and good debate on a very important subject. there was talk earlier about a ping-pong game going on. that ping-pong game is probably between the european parliament and two member states, so please do not use the commission as a ball. we are trying to have a coordinated, responsible and coherent response to everything relating to migration and borders because it all goes together. we cannot have a visa policy if we do not have border control. we cannot have credible protection of people who ask for asylum if we do not have a common asylum policy in the european union. we cannot have legal migration that works if we do not also work with integration and we cannot fight irregular migration if we do not have a proper and decent return and readmission policy. so, in order to have all this together, we need a clear framework and we need a european framework. the commission has therefore presented this communication. with all respect to the hard-working people in the commission, i will reveal a secret to you. we cannot produce a communication like this in two days. it is not possible. it has been planned for a long time. this is not a response to one or two presidents or prime ministers – this is something that we have been planning for a long time, and it is all there. those with whom we have been working together on a daily basis will know that since day one i have been working with them and the council to achieve a joint common european asylum system. it is hard work, it is difficult and we are working very slowly, but we are making some progress. we are working together on legal migration, we are trying to reinforce frontex, and i have been promising you a paper on integration since my hearing last february and, already last year, we proposed better governance of schengen. this is not a response to one or two prime ministers calling for something. it is something well thought out and it is something that will lead to further legislation and proposals in the light of the european council meeting in june, which will have as a theme – also planned for a long time – migration issues. of course, the situation in northern africa and in the mediterranean accelerates the need for us in europe to have our house in order. is that a reason to reinstall internal border control? no, of course not. is there a reason for european action? yes, there is. we have about 25 000 tunisians coming to europe. we have discussed this on many occasions here in the plenary. of course, every individual comes for a reason, namely that he – because it is very often a he – has no work in tunisia. i feel very strongly about every individual’s fate here, but not all of them can come to europe. it is much better – and that is why we are working with the tunisian authorities and italy in order to see how we can support italy to create jobs and growth – for these people to find a future in tunisia, because they are not refugees. however, there are refugees coming, and increasingly more so now. this week a lot of people have come from libya – third country nationals, even libyans – and that might increase. these people are clearly a reason for european action and solidarity. the commission has invited all member states to a conference on 12 may in order to discuss relocation and a prolongation of the malta project in order to assist malta with the thousands of people who have been going there. but we will also have the unhcr there, so we will try to ask member states to take increased responsibility for the refugees running away from the increasing violence in libya who are stranded in tunisia and at the border. turning to schengen, i agree with you – or most of you – who have said that schengen is a fantastic achievement. the fact that we can travel from finland to malta, from portugal to estonia, without ever showing a passport is a wonderful symbol of european integration. i want to protect this and further promote it. i am happy that i can count on your support in this. however, the system is not perfect. we knew long before all this started that there were some weaknesses in the systems. evaluation has not worked, because member states are evaluating each other and that is not a good thing. we need a european mechanism with the involvement of the european parliament. i presented this in november last year and i remember that i got quite a lot of support from this plenary to do this. we need to have tools to help the member states perform better in protecting eu external borders. we need to strengthen monitoring and we need more – not less – europe. so, in order to assess this situation and to decide on the necessary means, we really need a european approach. the events of last week have confirmed this. the shortcomings should never automatically lead to the reintroduction of border control. there has to be an assessment of the shortcomings in all other ways possible, such as providing financial and operational support. member states can also help each other. we are also working together with you on strengthening frontex. the point of departure is strengthening current legislation. i am convinced that the current rules can cater for most situations. where there are differences in interpretation, the commission should consult with member states in order to clarify the rules. this can be done by issuing guidelines or recommendations. there are particular circumstances where there might be a need to reintroduce border controls. that is already provided for today and it has been the case in a few situations – for example a major event such as a terrorist threat. there could be a major event where member states, under very clear circumstances, need to do this. but we need to strengthen the european dimension of this and to prevent member states from unilaterally taking action. that is what we are talking about. we live in turbulent times. many of the things that are happening are a reason for joy – in egypt and tunisia – but there are also a lot of concerns. we need to be calm in this situation. we need to try to handle it in the short term, but also in the long term. we need to strengthen our rules, not to undermine them. we need to strengthen the rules based on european law, on our values and on international commitments. we need a european leadership to stand up against simplistic solutions – and i have heard some of them here today – and populism. we need more europe, not less. , in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the free movement of persons within the eu is, along with the euro, one of the absolute pillars of the european project. there is no reason to question this today. the response to the thousands of refugees literally pouring into southern europe cannot be that we close our internal borders, even temporarily. the only response is to work towards a common european asylum and immigration policy in the short term. we cannot and will not accept that the arrival of 30,000 refugees on the shores of italy or greece will call into question the pillars of the eu. of course italy is right to call for european solidarity in tackling this problem. therein lies the solution. but blocking the internal borders, even temporarily, is a panic reaction unworthy of the eu leaders.
, in writing. italy's decision to issue temporary residence permits to thousands of tunisian immigrants arriving on its soil, followed by france's request to temporarily re-establish border controls, has called into question one of the most tangible elements of european integration: the schengen area. the commission's proposals in its communication of 4 may, which include an extension of the 'exceptional' circumstances which would allow the reintroduction of internal border controls, leave me somewhat perplexed. we are not going to put one of europe's finest achievements in jeopardy because of the will of two presidents! immigration is a challenge that requires a european response, and i therefore call for a common migration policy. it's time to take this case to the next level. i hope that at the european summit in june, when this issue will be discussed, populist sentiments will not pollute the atmosphere.

in writing. forests cover more than 42% of the union's territory. the wood sector accounts for more than two million jobs, mainly in smes, and a turnover of 300 billion euros. the forestry industry employs 350,000 people. the volume cut/increase ratio is stable in the union at around 60%, but projections suggest that this ratio will increase beyond 100% in several countries, causing a decrease in standing timber reserves after 2020! i am convinced that sustainable forest management is essential to maintaining the capacity of the union's forests to fulfil economic, ecological and social functions. that is why i have called on the commission to come forward with proposals to supplement regulation no 995/2010 on wood to ensure that all wood and wood products placed on the european market come from sustainably managed forests. the commission and the member states must make it compulsory to implement sustainable forest management in the union.
in writing. climate change and forests are inextricably linked. in the fight against climate change, the protection of forests is essential. forests could be better used in this fight, not only by preventing logging but also by afforestation and reforestation programmes. as a result of climate change, each forest type and forest sector is exposed to specific and unpredictable threats such as storms, droughts or fires. it is therefore crucial that the european union reinforces its strategy to combat these phenomena. sustainable forest management must seek to reconcile production and forest protection aspects. sustainable forest management is essential to maintain the capacity of forests to fulfil economic, ecological and social functions. greater attention to the maintenance, balance and enhancement of forest services is essential. the preservation of biodiversity must be one of the priorities of our political action.
in writing. it goes without saying that the protection of forests is a key environmental issue. well-managed forests are the main carbon sink and play a key role in the fight against climate change. on the other hand, undergoing intensive deforestation, they account for 25% of all emissions of co2, a greenhouse gas caused by human activities. the european union, including sweden and finland, which alone account for 33% of europe's forests, as well as the countries bordering the mediterranean, have an interest in strengthening their strategy to combat the phenomena that damage forests, such as air pollution and fires. in this context, i welcome the adoption, in the context of the vote on the green paper on 'preparing forests for climate change', of paragraph 38 of the arsenis report, which 'urges the commission to submit a legislative proposal for the protection of forests against fire' and in particular envisages 'a ban on all construction for 30 years on land that has been affected by a forest fire'. this is a good way to counteract the widespread practice of arson for the purpose of real estate promotion.

- i'm the reporter. - mr president, commissioner, if the plenary, hopefully by a large majority, approves the agreement we have negotiated between the institutions, we will be witnessing an important moment for the transport sector in europe, a milestone which could guide policy for the next decades. the immediate, concrete impact on the ground will of course depend on the political will of the member states to take advantage of the new opportunities. we're not imposing anything. we are only making things possible and in particular the application of a principle which we have been advocating for a number of years as a parliament, namely 'the polluter pays', the internalisation of external costs. some of us who are veterans know that we have been fighting hard for this since 2006, when mrs wortmann-kool led the last revision. in 2008 a commission proposal followed, which we have been working on for three years. those who have followed the case closely know how difficult it has been to achieve this result. it is a compromise, a compromise between the institutions, but also a compromise within the institutions, supported, for example, by the smallest possible majority in the council, but also opposed here in parliament. some think it is not ambitious enough and others think it is all going too far. it is the merit of the negotiating team and especially of the shadow rapporteurs who, together with myself, people from the council and the commission, have reached this delicate balance. i ask each of you to support the package we have achieved as a step in the right direction. it gives member states the opportunity for the first time to add noise and air pollution to the existing infrastructure charges, which are not yet applied consistently everywhere, in such a way as to encourage fleet renewal. at the same time, it allows member states to achieve more variation in the charge depending on the time of day the truck is on the road. this gives the authorities control over the way in which mobility is improved. at the same time, there is also a strong commitment, the strongest possible commitment, by member states to reinvest revenues in the transport system to make it more sustainable and to reinvest at least 15% of revenues in the trans-european transport network. at the same time - and this was an important question from the european parliament - there is clarity on the transparency requirement. member states must explain the level of revenue from these charges and what they will do with it to improve the transport system. the package will also be applied to a larger part of the fleet, in particular all vehicles over 3,5 tonnes. that is the principle, that is the norm, that is the agreement. it will also be applied to the whole motorway network. we have emphasized the importance of the interoperability of the system. one box per truck to cross europe, not 25 or 26. that's enshrined in the legislation. the commission has already made a number of proposals. we had quite a discussion about that. the solution we have found in the form of a number of declarations by the three institutions is sufficient to establish no precedent. in conclusion, the eurovignette is not a panacea. we are not going to solve the mobility problem completely with this, of course not. it is an important part of a solution to a more sustainable transport system. price incentives will be an important element of that, but we will have to do much more than that. but it is a step in the right direction and i and my colleagues ask for your support.

in writing. the main mission of the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction (emcdda) is to collect information on drugs and drug addiction in order to produce and disseminate objective, reliable and comparable data at european level. the emcdda is, in fact, open to any third country which shares the interests of the eu. croatia had been applying for it since 2005. it will also be part of the european information network on drugs and drug addiction. for me, this report also reflects the need to improve the exchange of data between member states and european agencies and, above all, to prepare for possible accession in a more measured way than the 'great' enlargement to the countries of central and eastern europe (ceecs) that took place in 2004 and 2007.
in writing. the primary objective of the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction (emcdda) is to collect data on drugs and drug addiction in order to prepare and publish objective, reliable and comparable information at european level. the republic of croatia will thus participate in the observatory's work programme, be linked to the european information network on drugs and drug addiction (reitox) and share data with the emcdda. the republic of croatia is a transit zone for drugs from producer countries and remains one of the main transit points for drug trafficking to the european union. however, in 2010 it adopted a programme to implement an action plan to combat drug addiction and a national prevention programme for young people. the training of police officers and the provision of necessary equipment also continued. croatia's participation in the emcdda will thus enable it to understand and better deal with this problem through an exchange of information. this participation is also an encouraging signal for croatia's forthcoming accession to the european union.
in writing. the objective of this proposal is to extend the scope of the proposal for a regulation on the crossborder transport of euro cash by road between member states in the euro area (main proposal) to the territory of member states which are about to adopt the euro. the period before the changeover to the euro leads to an increased need to transport euro cash. i welcome this extension of the scope (although it should be noted that the legal basis here is article 352 tfeu, which means that the european parliament has only the power of approval).
in writing. global navigation satellite systems (gnss) applications are a central and indispensable component of activity in all transport-related fields and their proper functioning makes transport safer, more environmentally friendly and more economical. the european union cannot remain dependent on systems originally designed for other purposes by other countries. given the high added value of the gnss and galileo projects to european industrial policy, their success is essential. a targeted action plan is the best option to provide new momentum and make a significant contribution to safety and environmental objectives and to improving the flow of traffic for road transport. in addition, satellite navigation systems must ensure interoperability between different systems, including conventional systems. the extension of the egnos system coverage must be a priority. it must then be extended to the whole of the european continent, but also to the euro-mediterranean partnership countries, as well as to the middle east and africa. finally, the commission should propose measures to ensure a sufficient level of funding without affecting other funds allocated to transport policy.
in writing. the european parliament today approved by a large majority the revision of the eurovignette directive. the text provides that heavy goods vehicles will pay for air pollution and noise pollution. the agreement approved today allows member states to charge road hauliers for the cost of air and noise pollution, in addition to the price of using motorway infrastructure. this is an important revision, but it is only a small step in the right direction. because the regulations are not binding! i am therefore still waiting for new proposals which make these new measures compulsory by including the cost of all environmental damage and extend the polluter pays principle to all modes of transport. the text also insists that the revenue from toll collection be effectively used. on this point, parliament obliged the member states to invest part of the revenue from tolling in improving road infrastructure and mobility. it should also be possible to extend these sampling to projects such as reducing air pollution and noise pollution.
in writing. i voted in favour of this compromise on the revision of the 'euro-vignette' directive, the aim of which is to introduce the 'polluter pays' principle for heavy goods vehicles on motorways. the member states will finally be able to include in their taxes or tolls the real costs of air and noise pollution from road transport, whereas only infrastructure costs could be taken into account until now. the compromise falls short of the european parliament's ambitions and will not, on its own, revolutionise road transport, whose sector and member states are clearly not yet ready to shoulder the real cost of the ecological footprint. the average additional cost should not exceed 4 cents per vehicle per kilometre, and trucks with the cleanest engines and operating in off-peak hours would be exempt. but this reform was on the back burner before the belgian presidency put it back on the council's table. and this is a step forward that i welcome, a positive first step towards more sustainable road transport.
in writing. this proposal for a regulation dates back to a decision of the european council of june 2006. at the time, the eu decided to extend the existing national accounts and the statistical data to be collected to the main aspects of sustainable development. to complement national accounts and data, the commission has proposed a regulation to establish european environmental economic accounts. in accordance with the commission's proposal, the member states should therefore be provided with a common methodology and accounting standards, definitions, classifications and rules, which should be brought together in a framework binding on each of them. although i believe that priority should first be given to data already available (i.e. collected at regional, national and european level), i am of the opinion that if the need for these additional modules is proven, does not generate unnecessary bureaucracy and additional costs, in this case eurostat should be allowed to collect data from member states for the creation of economic and environmental accounts at european level. that is why i also welcomed the establishment of these new european environmental economic accounts and proposed to extend their scope to other modules.

in writing. since the financial and economic crisis, they have been the talk of the town: credit rating agencies (cras). but what about their now indispensable role? the european parliament has dealt with the matter. while rating agencies have several interesting functions (such as centralising information on the credit quality of issuers, which is particularly useful in our globalised world, etc.), in fact, the evolution of the regulatory framework has elevated these 'information intermediaries' into 'regulatory authorities'! but that is a pitfall to be avoided! the financial crisis has highlighted the three major problems in the sector: the lack of competition, the excessive reliance on external ratings in the regulatory framework and the fact that ncas are not legally responsible for their ratings.

in writing. today, parliament adopted the revised text of my colleague andré schwab's consumer rights directive. i welcome the adoption of this directive, which will strengthen the basis of common consumer protection rules, particularly as regards the sale of goods online. i also welcome the fact that the legislator has left member states the possibility of providing for more consumer-friendly measures in their respective national laws. however, like many consumer associations, i regret that options have been set up to allow member states to derogate from certain provisions of the directive for commercial or sectoral purposes.
in writing. a well-protected consumer is a secure citizen and a sign of the maturity of our modern democracies. this is where the directive adopted today is important. not a day goes by without the european consumer, when making a purchase online or accepting a modification to a telephone subscription contract, being confronted with a question about the conformity of the signed or approved contract. in response to the often unbalanced relationship between traders and consumers, the european parliament has negotiated essential rights, including: - a 14-day right of withdrawal, whether the purchase was made on the internet, by e-mail, by telephone or by a salesperson. - if the seller has not informed the buyer of the right of withdrawal, the purchased item may be returned up to one year after the date of purchase. - all deliveries must be made within 30 days. after this period, the buyer may withdraw without giving any reason. the vote comes after tough negotiations between parliament and the member states, and is a clear signal that the same rights should be exercised throughout the union.
in writing. the directive adopted today by a very large majority in the european parliament marks an important step towards better consumer protection in the european union. the new rules will considerably strengthen consumer rights, in particular with regard to information, delivery and termination of contracts. the right of withdrawal is extended to 14 days for all european citizens, which is a major step forward. but if there is one area where the directive is innovative, it is in the exercise of consumer rights in online commerce: the prohibition of pre-ticked boxes, complete information on the different costs are all consumer protection tools.
in writing. i welcome the vote on this report. the strengthening of nuclear safety and security rules was necessary for several reasons. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's nuclear waste disposal system is not disrupted by the nuclear accident in japan, but also because the so-called 'highly active and long-lived' radioactive waste is still being stored on a temporary basis. spent fuel is usually stored safely near reactors, but it is clear that for permanent storage the level of safety should be much higher. so it is our responsibility to demand maximum security! that is why i also voted for the amendment to ban nuclear waste management facilities in seismic or coastal areas with a high risk of sea level rise and tsunamis. i also support the polluter pays principle and i also voted in favour of the amendment calling for cost assessment, monitoring, regular reporting to the european commission and the involvement of national parliaments.
in writing. it was important that the european parliament gave an opinion on the revision of the radioactive waste directive. it is a sign of responsibility and maturity to ignore differences on whether to maintain or abandon nuclear power and to reject an effective policy of disposing of nuclear waste. that is the first lesson of today's vote. clearly, nuclear safety is also about strengthening the rules on nuclear safety and security in the post-fukushima scenario. i particularly welcome the adoption of amendments nos 124 and 130 which call for a ban on nuclear waste management facilities in seismically hazardous or coastal areas and for the development of a safety briefing to accompany any radioactive waste management activity. it is to be hoped that the european energy ministers will hear this strong message in favour of a culture of safety. this necessarily requires that priority be given to deep-burial solutions, such as permanent dry rock storage or permanent storage in deep cavities (3 000 to 5 000 m deep), which are still being studied. and the use of transportation as the ultimate solution for highly radioactive waste.
in writing. - i abstained on the vote on the cizelj report following a proposal from the european commission to lay down rules on the management of radioactive waste. - why? - why? i did not vote against because this outcome gives commissioner oettinger the opportunity to stick to his original proposal and to ban the export of radioactive material to third countries. this is against the wishes of a number of member states who would like to see the existing ban on such exports lifted. i am not sure that the commissioner has been able to give us a clear answer to this question, but i am sure that he will be able to give us a clear answer to this question. moreover, if the eu wants to use nuclear energy, it must manage its own nuclear waste. what some member states want is to border on european public crime. it is regrettable that the export of spent nuclear fuel to russia and ukraine for reprocessing is not prohibited. the european green group welcomes the fact that a majority of meps rejected further exports and approved a green amendment banning the storage of radioactive waste in seismic zones. but i could not vote for this report either because the rules proposed are far too weak.
in writing. the cap needed to be revised to better address the challenges of food security, climate change, sustainable management of natural resources, maintenance of the natural environment and maintaining a vibrant rural economy. the sector had to be made more competitive and the cap more equitable, green, cost-effective and efficient. it had to be formulated in a way that was understandable to all, not just farmers but also consumers and taxpayers. the report is moving in the right direction, doing everything possible to make agriculture a more dynamic and competitive sector, to be better able to meet the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. in addition, the report provides for adequate budgetary resources to be maintained after 2013, which is a victory in itself.
in writing. the common agricultural policy is the only genuine european policy. it has long been a shield against shortages and sectoral crises, but it is no longer the refuge for farmers and their families who are suffering the full effects of the volatility of commodity prices and global competition. i would like to see the continuing decline in farms in belgium and the dramatic fall in employment (down 56% in 30 years). the cap must therefore be reformed to meet the challenges of today's production and food security, environmental protection and renewable energy production. the report which was voted on this afternoon takes up, and this is good news, the broad lines laid down by the european commission in favour of a gradual reform based on a more balanced, more targeted aid system with a marked 'ecological' orientation. it is obvious that we must set up rules to regulate the market and help small farms, which have so far been the big losers in successive reforms. this is the only way to give young people hope, to motivate them to take over the family farms, to convince them that agriculture is simply a sector of the future.
in writing. − the future cap must guarantee access to healthy and locally produced food for all. i am in favour of family farms, of stable and fair prices for farmers and consumers, of a shift towards sustainable and social agriculture respecting the limits of our natural resources. i am voting for an end to dumping european surplus production on markets in the south because this market-disrupting practice is putting the knife to the local producers in the south. they cannot compete with the underpriced imports from europe. we need to shift livestock production to animal-friendly and ecological production, ending our dependence on imported soybeans for animal feed. that is why i voted for all the amendments limiting subsidies per person per company. that is why i voted in favour of the amendments which provide for a greening of subsidies. that is why i supported the amendments which favour organic 'low input' farming. that is why i supported the amendments which restrict the large concentration of power in the market in favour of agribusiness and retail. that is why i supported the amendments which favour small family farms and voted against the worst mass import of soya beans in europe. that's why i'm voting for food sovereignty.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. we shall soon establish in a legally binding manner the conditions under which member states may restrict or prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. we are advocating a system of liability whereby the polluter pays for the damage caused by the deliberate introduction of gmos. member states may prohibit or restrict gmos on the basis of additional environmental motives, such as the prevention of pesticide resistance in weeds or pests, such as the preservation of local biodiversity, such as scientific uncertainty about the possible negative effects of gmos, such as the socio-economic impact and the excessive cost of coexistence of conventional organic and gmo agriculture. it is essentially a matter of protecting the autonomy of farmers and consumers, against the notion that anything is technically possible, against the belief that everything in this world is for sale. this report balances the debate on respect for the environment and the socioeconomic survival of farmers, and that is why i support the report by mrs lepage.

in writing. wherever you are in the european union, you can reach the emergency services by dialling 112, the single european emergency number. however, only 26% of eu citizens are able to spontaneously identify 112 as the emergency number in the eu. the commission and the member states should therefore step up their information campaigns to make the 112 emergency call number known to all union citizens and persons travelling there, and organise and support public promotion and awareness-raising activities. it is also essential to ensure that every segment of society has access to this service, including people with disabilities. there is a need to significantly improve the accuracy and reliability of caller location information. emergency response agencies need to ensure better coordination between themselves, both at national, cross-border and european level, in order to achieve the highest level of efficiency. it is also necessary to establish performance indicators for the quality of the 112 service, taking into account in particular the needs for accessibility, multilingualism and quality and timely interventions.
in writing. awareness and reliability are the two messages that the vote on the resolution on 112 - the european emergency number - sent this afternoon. first of all, make the 112 number known, which is free and accessible throughout europe. that's the biggest challenge. the task is immense when we consider that only 26% of europeans identify 112 as the number of emergency services in the union, with huge disparities between member states. and it is precisely these member states that can fill this gap through comprehensive and targeted campaigns of awareness, information and promotion. reliability, in particular with regard to the precise and automatic location of the caller. this is invaluable information to ensure the best possible response from first responders. everyone knows the urgent need for a reliable emergency number, both at home and abroad. much has been done, but much remains to be done to make 112 a reflex for every european citizen facing an emergency.
in writing. - the european parliament has today drawn clear lessons from the global credit crisis and the european debt crisis. it voted to ban uncovered credit default swaps (cds) on government bonds and to restrict naked short selling. credit default swaps insure bondholders against payment problems of governments and corporations. however, these derivatives are also bought by speculators who do not themselves own bonds. those who hold credit default swaps without an underlying interest benefit from panic in the financial markets. because when there is growing doubt about a country's ability to pay its debts, the cds increases in value. the wind trade in cds has not caused the debt crisis of greece and other euro countries, but has greatly exacerbated it. speculators are only allowed to buy greek cds if they also actually own greek government bonds. that makes it harder to bet on a greek bankruptcy. speculators in the financial markets profit too easily from this kind of perverse trade, while european taxpayers bleed. i am therefore pleased that the european parliament has adopted the proposal to ban the holding of uncovered cds on government bonds. i hope that the council of ministers will be convinced of this in the forthcoming negotiations.
in writing. i welcome the vote on the corinne lepage report, which is before meps today for first reading, because it aims to provide legal certainty to member states wishing to restrict or ban gmos on their territory. the report gives them a wide range of arguments to justify their decision and goes further than the original proposal of the european commission, whose recent positions on gmos are well known. i asked commissioner dalli why the existing legislation on this subject - namely directive 2001/18/ec - which contains many legal and scientific safeguards, was still not being applied. why have the recommendations contained in the conclusions of the agriculture council of december 2008, inter alia in terms of strengthening scientific evaluations at community level, remained unfulfilled until now? i believe that the guarantee of an independent and irrefutable scientific evaluation is an essential precondition for the confidence of citizens and member states. overall, i really consider today's vote a victory for the citizens, because let's not forget that according to the last eurobarometer in october 2010, 61% of europeans are still opposed to gmo cultivation!
in writing. i congratulate corinne lepage on her report. she was able to determine specific conditions for the opt-out. the report has the merit of improving legal certainty and eliminating litigation. it does not alter the centralised authorisation procedure of efsa, but recognises the right of member states to carry out additional national assessments or to broaden the basis of their risk management measures. although it is not intended to determine whether europe should be for or against the cultivation of gmos, i would like to stress that we cannot oppose research and development of new technologies. i am therefore pleased to note that the report provides for the possibility of allocating the necessary financial resources for scientific research. the same is true of the union's credibility in r & d and the competitiveness of european companies in relation to the rest of the world (64 million hectares of gmos are planted in the united states, 21 million hectares of gmos in india and canada).
in writing. the european parliament, by adopting this afternoon the report by corinne lepage on measures to ban the cultivation of gmos in the national territory of the member states, has just corrected an error made by the european commission. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly aspects of the production of foodstuffs. it must be said that gmos remain a divisive issue at eu level. with obvious consequences: the cultivation of genetically modified plants continues to decline in europe: -23% in 2010 compared to 2008. this is another reason to complete the eu's authorisation system for gmo cultivation. it should also be borne in mind that to restore citizens' confidence, it is crucial to set effective criteria that respond to their concerns about the environment. the aim is to address the concerns of farmers who have opted for conventional or organic farming in the face of the risk of contamination of their fields by genetically modified varieties.
in writing. - mr president, like my group, i voted against the amended lepage report. the debate on gmos in parliament is always emotionally charged. the debate we are having today should be a debate, not for or against gmos, but about whether we want to give member states more flexibility if they want to restrict or ban their use. the package adopted today is a step backwards because it is fragmenting the single market. environment and health are by definition problems that we should tackle together. environment and health do not stop at the borders of the member states. i therefore call for a strengthened european approach with a stronger role for the efsa. we must be careful that we do not introduce a de facto 'ban on gmos' by unnecessarily extending the criteria for banning or restricting gmos. i would argue for a case-by-case approach, i.e. that gmos are allowed if it is scientifically proven that the genetically modified substance is as safe as the non-modified food. the research on gmos must also be continued, but it must be done in a scientifically responsible way, not on the basis of political dogmas.
in writing. freedom, democracy, equality, non-discrimination and respect for fundamental rights are core values for the european union. each member state of the union must ensure that these fundamental rights are respected, protected and promoted. while we denounce the violation of civil liberties and democratic control, and discrimination, including on the basis of sexual orientation, when these rights are not respected outside the union, we must also express our concern when these same rights are threatened within the union itself. while it is true that the adoption of a new constitution falls within national competence, it is nevertheless the duty of all member states, present and future, to respect the values of the european union, the european charter of fundamental rights and the european convention on human rights in letter and spirit. the european commission must uphold these values and ensure that european citizens have the assurance that our values are indeed at the heart of our legislation.
in writing. i agree with the objective of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. i think this is an issue that should not be politicized, so there should be no left-right split on this issue! we must prevent global warming of 2 degrees. however, the current crisis situation is also a real obstacle to the environmental progress announced before the economic crisis. and while i wish for this ambitious goal to be achieved, for the sake of the planet and future generations, i have doubts about its feasibility, although i hope i am wrong.
in writing. i unfortunately had to vote against the eickout report, which was considerably watered down by the plenary session this afternoon and the adoption of epp amendments falling short of the so-called "3x20" targets of the energy/climate package adopted in 2008. these are objectives that are not only aimed at combating climate change and protecting the health of future generations, but also at facilitating investment in innovation and future technologies. this vote is all the more regrettable because it goes against the choice of a part of european industry, which has already made the bet on a low-carbon society. in addition, the number of jobs in eco-industries is very encouraging: 3.4 million people currently, a figure that would be "boosted" with the eu's climate target being raised to 30%. the estimated creation of 6 million additional jobs in europe is also worth mentioning. the commission and the member states must not therefore turn their backs on their ambitious climate change objectives, or fall behind certain us states and china, which are surely converting to green technologies.
in writing. - this report sets out the precise points for the future: crossborder work and initiatives are among the most important engines of european integration. the control of expenditure and the european added value in practice must be strengthened. this also means that the co-financing of the länder and regions must be fully clarified in advance of the applications. the commission's proposal is to set up a european network of national experts to assist the member states in the implementation of the community's environmental policy.
in writing. the goerens report, which i voted for today, deals with the impact of budget support, the consistency of the eligibility criteria and the accompanying measures to strengthen the political dialogue between the european union and developing countries. the report highlights, on the basis of an assessment of global budget support in seven developing countries, that budget support can be an effective means of facilitating developing countries' strategies to eradicate poverty while enhancing the ownership and accountability of their governments, particularly in the management of their public finances. the report notes, however, that the commission's control mechanisms for the beneficiary countries need to be strengthened. this is why there is a need to involve parliaments and civil society more in the dialogue on poverty reduction policies and annual budget support reviews. finally, i took the opportunity to stress once again the need for coherence in development policies and to reiterate my wish that the cfsp should focus on the promotion of democracy and human rights, which are key conditions for sustainable development.
in writing. i am in favour of budget support because it increases the resources of the recipient state to implement its own budget according to its own procedures and, above all, according to its own policy choices. budget support strengthens governance by providing for debate and dialogue upstream, at the level of the state and its regulatory functions in particular. it increases the coherence of the national budget and, above all, it makes the states responsible for the priorities and results it sets. it allows each country to take full ownership of its own development. under the 10th edf, budget support rose from 25% to almost 50% of the aid allocated to the acp over five years. i would remind those who are wary of this type of aid that budget support cannot be implemented in all countries and in all circumstances. the eligibility criteria are specific and are assessed before the finalisation of a budget support programme, during its implementation and, above all, before each disbursement. a rapid alert system has been put in place to identify any slippage. in the event of abuse or fraud, the state must reimburse the sums which have been the subject of irregularities.
in writing. - budget support is an appropriate instrument for development cooperation, but it also has pitfalls. for example, beneficiary countries must have adequate own contributions in the areas of poverty reduction, macroeconomic management, public financial management and governance before they can receive budget support. in reality, there are huge differences between the recipient countries. budget support must be linked to a strong political dialogue. the leading role of the national parliaments of the recipient countries, civil society organisations and local government bodies is crucial. they are best placed to define the priority sectors, prepare the country strategy papers and monitor the budget allocations. in order to strengthen parliamentary control, national parliaments should consult with civil society organisations. the report calls for a system of information exchange between civil society and public opinion with a view to the follow-up of budget support. budget support, like programmed aid, should be seen as a transitional instrument and should not prejudice efforts to improve the ability of countries to raise their own resources, such as taxes, to break the dependence on donations from third countries. budget support may even be reduced in certain cases (emerging or oil and mineral rich countries).
in writing. − social services of general interest are essential social and economic pillars of our societies and provide a necessary counterbalance to an overly narrow economic interpretation of the internal market. they are the expression of a social europe because they promote social cohesion and guarantee social inclusion. to be clear, social services are not just for the most deprived but for all eu citizens. the lack of a clear legal framework leaves the court of justice with every latitude to interpret these services of general interest through case law. it's a very bad evolution. europe does not want legislation at the moment, whereas it is necessary to look for the means to finance these services adequately and to find guarantees for the employment they generate. the report by the proinsias de rossa rightly denounces these elements and that is why i supported it. yet it opens the door to private-public partnerships and privatization of these services. unjustly, because the liberalization of telecommunications, post, rail, etc. has not led to better services at an affordable price. - no, it's the opposite. that is why i fully supported the alternative resolution by the greens, which calls for separate legislation for these social services and thus puts a real social europe at the forefront.
in writing. official development assistance is necessary and cannot be reduced under any circumstances. there is no reason why we should not honour our commitments to allocate 0.7% of gdp to oda. however, the quality of the implementation, management and use of official development assistance needs to be improved in order to maximise its impact on growth and poverty reduction. official development assistance amounts to over 120 billion dollars. doing more and doing better goes beyond an increase in resources. i am in favour of 'more' general or sectoral budget support and fewer projects when macroeconomic and governance criteria allow it. when a country is eligible for 30% budget support, why should it not be eligible for 90%? it is necessary to recognize that, beyond the fragmentation and proliferation of actors, the international community faces a new challenge: the transformation of aid. we must realize that there are other types of relations, other ways of doing things and other ways of acting, which must now be taken into account, besides paris and accra. the response to these changes can only be inclusive and political.
