vice-president of the commission. − mr president, unusually i have plenty of time today, but i shall try to be as short as possible. first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr de grandes pascual, for this exhaustive and balanced report. the threat to civil aviation is real. we were reminded last october that some people are still seeking to target aviation and we were reminded that we are vulnerable. with regard to security scanners, the parliament resolution of october 2008 asked the commission to analyse the impact of security scanners on fundamental rights and health aspects. a basis for discussion with parliament and council, addressing some essential issues concerning the use of security scanners at eu airports, was provided by the communication of 15 june 2010. the commission has since continued to assess all aspects and is now ready to come forward with a legislative proposal on security scanners. on the basis of the de grandes pascual report, we can now move forward quickly: some airports are keen to start using scanners to improve our security. this will allow member states and airports to use security scanners at eu airports. it will also lay down strict operational and detection performance criteria. today, security scanners are a valid alternative to existing screening methods, in particular at large airports with major passenger flows. what is more, current technology allows full respect of fundamental rights and health concerns. further, scanners have good detection performance, as both metallic and non-metallic items can be detected. moreover, experience shows that they are increasingly accepted by passengers and staff as a convenient method of screening. at this stage, however, to safeguard the health and safety of passengers and staff, only security scanners that do not use ionising radiation should be allowed. the commission has therefore asked its scientific committee on emerging and newly identified health risks to assess the effects of security scanners that use ionising radiation on human health. the commission has also proposed for passengers to be given the possibility of opting out from a security scan and of undergoing alternative screening methods. we are convinced that a common eu approach addresses the current fragmented situation while ensuring both the highest level of security and the best possible protection for fundamental rights and health. with regard to liquids, the deadline of 29 april 2011 was intended to be set for the first step towards abolishing the restrictions on liquids on board aircraft. however, this step proved impossible to implement for several reasons. the commission therefore decided to remove this obligation and to instead focus on 29 april 2013. this is the legal deadline on which all restrictions on liquids must be lifted. however, airports can start the screening of liquids before that date, and are encouraged to do so. in this context you also wanted the commission to make a statement on liquids. let me assure you that the commission is fully committed to ensuring that the 2013 deadline is met. therefore, a working group consisting of member states, the aviation industry and international partners will be set up and will start work right after the summer. this group will agree on concrete steps to be taken in the coming year and will coordinate implementation, including operational trials at airports. international cooperation, in particular with the united states, is essential to prevent a similar situation in 2013. the 2013 deadline has also been endorsed by most of the 60 icao states applying liquid restrictions. on 22 june 2011, the eu and the us signed a joint statement, agreeing to closely work together towards the 2013 deadline. the joint statement demonstrates our common acknowledgement and acceptance of the 2013 deadline, and includes an agreement to exchange information on operational trials and on planned regulatory requirements. let me now go back to the de grandes pascual report and turn to cargo. last december, the council endorsed the high-level working group report and action plan on strengthening air cargo security. this was a direct response to the october incident involving explosive devices concealed in air cargo consignments from yemen. i welcome parliament’s support to this work, as expressed in the de grandes pascual report. as regards progress on implementing the action plan, the commission is developing a common eu risk assessment for cargo security, with input from interior ministries and the intelligence services. and we are working within icao to set global standards and coordinate capacity-building activities in third countries. this is on-going work and we should continue to give it the necessary priority. unfortunately, i am as yet unable to report on a successful conclusion to the new rule-making for cargo. at the meeting of experts in the regulatory committee on 8 june 2011, member state delegates failed to give sufficient support to the commission proposal, due to a large number of abstentions, which came as a big surprise. at the transport council in june, i asked ministers to ensure that improved rules on cargo can be adopted as soon as possible. i am hopeful that this will be possible. the commission is therefore resubmitting the proposals to the regulatory committee this week. it is important that the eu takes action to close a clear security gap for air cargo arriving from third countries. i would like to thank parliament for its attention to the various components of this file. your careful scrutiny has led to better legislation and therefore better protection of citizens.

in writing. the right to the protection of personal data is recognised by the treaty on the functioning of the european union and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. in early november 2010, the european commission published its 'comprehensive data protection strategy for the european union' with a view to revising the data protection directive. the european parliament, which wishes to take part in this debate and influence the revision of the data protection directive, has drawn up a report. this document, which was voted almost unanimously in the libe committee, reflects my concerns. i believe that citizens should be able to control their information, have access to their data, change it and delete it. these are, in my view, fundamental rights that must be guaranteed in our digital society. the right to be forgotten must exist for every citizen.
in writing. in the digital age, technology allows us to create, store, and send vast amounts of data. stopping this technological revolution is illusory. the risk of a breach of data protection provisions is therefore real and can pose serious risks to the fundamental rights of individuals. first of all, it is essential to raise awareness and educate citizens, especially young people, about the wise use of technology. the emphasis must be on strengthening existing measures and we must commit ourselves to a comprehensive approach. the high level of protection of data subjects and the specific protection of vulnerable persons, in particular children, should be further consolidated and strengthened. it will also be necessary to improve the modalities and awareness of the exercise of the rights of access, rectification, erasure and blocking of data, and to ensure that citizens are able to exercise their rights. it should nevertheless be stressed that the data protection regime, while not being a hindrance to the protection of privacy and data, must keep administrative and financial burdens to a minimum, especially for smes.

in writing. the european parliament voted today on a report on crossborder exchanges of information on road traffic offences. 31 000 people are still killed and 300 000 seriously injured on european roads every year. 30% of these accidents are caused by speeding by drivers who live in a country other than the one in which they committed the road traffic offence! in addition, many crossborder road traffic offences go unpunished. the european parliament therefore calls for the country of origin of the driver involved in a serious road accident to be informed in order to ensure effective repression of the offence, in order to protect road users. the obstacles to crossborder cooperation remain significant, including the lack of police cooperation between member states. this report is therefore a first step towards crossborder cooperation such as that which already exists between belgium, the netherlands, germany and luxembourg.
in writing. by adopting this report on eu legislation on transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (tses) and related controls of feed and food, the european parliament has dealt a "knife blow" to the moral contract binding it to european citizens. he did, however, put an end to a 15-year ban. a decision taken in 1996 in the wake of the mad cow crisis (bovine spongiform encephalopathy (bse)). the vote this afternoon (485 votes to 162) sends the exact opposite message to what not only a majority of consumers but also farmers, distributors and food manufacturers want to hear. all these direct actors opposed the reintroduction of animal flours. yet nothing has changed in 15 years; scientific uncertainties remain, particularly for farmed fish, and there is no guarantee of effective traceability at european level to trace the origin of animal by-products flours. in conclusion, until the commission writes in black and white that animal meal poses no health safety problem, the 27 agriculture ministers will have to oppose a food policy which the citizens of europe no longer want.
in writing. - the commission proposed some time ago to lift provisions prohibiting the use of processed animal protein in feed for non-ruminants. the ep calls for strict conditions. the treated slaughterhouse waste may only come from species not associated with tse diseases. the production and sterilisation methods used for the treatment of slaughterhouse waste must meet the highest safety standards. the prohibition on recycling within the species ('cannibalism') should remain in force. the treatment of slaughter waste of different species should be completely separated. the separation of these production channels should be ensured by the competent authorities in the member states and monitored by the commission. before the ban on meat and bone meal is lifted, a reliable species-specific method should be applied to identify the animal species from which the proteins in feed originate, in order to prevent 'cannibalism' and the feeding of animal meal to ruminants. finally, the production of processed animal protein from category 1 or category 2 material is prohibited. only category 3 material suitable for human consumption may be used for the production of processed animal protein. only strict compliance with these conditions can lead to the lifting of the ban on meat and bone meal.
in writing. i am obviously disappointed with the outcome of this vote, because while the reintroduction of animal meal can be a solution to the current eu protein deficit, it is also true that the food security of europeans must be a priority. moreover, if we have to take into account the scientific and economic data relating to the use of animal flour, we must also respect the expectations of the europeans. in the midst of the health psychosis of e. coli, the question of consumer acceptability is quite understandable. the spectre of bovine spongiform encephalopathy and the associated images of hundreds of mad cows being slaughtered, with the added fear of the creutzfeldt-jakob variant, should make us extremely cautious and responsible. that is why i voted against this motion for a resolution.
in writing. - following the attacks in new york, london and madrid, airport security has been greatly tightened. it's absolutely necessary to thwart any possible attacks. but there are limits to what is permitted. the report on the use of security scanners at airports has fortunately been considerably improved in terms of privacy protection. the report does not express a clear preference for body scanners, but other technologies can also be used for security research. all of these must guarantee the health of passengers and their fundamental rights. therefore, data resulting from such research should be used only in that capacity and should be deleted immediately for privacy reasons. for example, no profiles may be used. screening should be random and certainly not selective. finally, x-ray technology is prohibited for health reasons for both passengers and workers. our group has also succeeded in forcing a revision of the land-use directive. as the report has been largely improved by green amendments, i have given it my full support.

we have a lot of instruments. there are many instruments that can be used today in a more coherent and effective way for democracy. we have the instrument of the democracy and human rights initiative, but we also have the possibility, under the lisbon treaty, of making better use of our trade agreements; we have the stability instrument, we have a whole series of instruments. now, is that enough? in writing. the right to freedom of movement is one of the most fundamental and visible rights conferred on citizens of the union. the creation of the schengen area and the integration of the schengen acquis into the framework of the union represent one of the greatest achievements of the european integration process. freedom of movement has become and must remain one of the pillars of european citizenship. therefore any further derogation from the current provisions or reintroduction, even exceptionally, of border controls will not be in the interests of strengthening the schengen system and will be contrary to the letter and spirit of the treaties and the acquis communautaire. the conditions for the temporary and exceptional reintroduction of internal border controls are already clearly set out in the schengen borders code. it is essential to strengthen schengen governance in order to ensure that each member state is able to control its external borders of the union and to strengthen mutual trust. there is also a need for greater solidarity with member states facing large flows of migrants.

in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the european union's external border management agency which introduces new rules. since 2005, frontex has been responsible for coordinating police activities at the eu's external borders. it was time to evaluate the first six years in order to strengthen it and make it more effective. i welcome the fact that the agency is no longer dependent on the member states for the purchase or lease of equipment (vehicles, helicopters, etc.). in addition, member states are legally obliged to fulfil their commitments to provide staff or equipment to the agency on an annual basis. i am satisfied with the fact that mechanisms have been put in place to ensure that the fundamental rights of migrants are respected, in particular through the appointment of a 'fundamental rights officer' and the development of a code of conduct. in accordance with international law, no migrant may be disembarked or handed over to the authorities of a state in which his life or liberty is threatened. it may seem obvious, but sometimes it's good to remember!
in writing. the new frontex rules adopted today will make the agency more visible and effective. this is a major reform of the agency since its creation. national guards, designated by the member states to take part in the missions, will reinforce the european border guard teams. the agency may also buy or lease its own equipment. the establishment of mechanisms to guarantee respect for fundamental rights is an important achievement in this area. the appointment of a fundamental rights officer and the creation of a consultative forum will make it possible to monitor the respect for fundamental rights in all frontex activities. it should also be emphasised that frontex will have to develop codes of conduct to ensure respect for human rights in all operations, including return operations, paying particular attention to unaccompanied minors and vulnerable persons.
in writing. the adoption of this resolution clearly indicates our desire to be kept informed of any measures concerning the implementation of this agreement, which has a dual commercial and environmental dimension, since its main objective is to 'promote the expansion and diversification of international trade in tropical timber from forests managed and harvested in a sustainable manner and to promote the sustainable management of tropical timber-producing forests'. global warming requires strict measures to ensure environmental governance that respects natural resources and contributes to the sustainable development of the planet. it is estimated that 20% of wood imports into the union are from illegal sources. none of the major tropical forestry regions is exempt the information requested by the european parliament is crucial because this issue is at the heart of the challenges facing the world as a whole, such as global warming, food security, the fight against poverty (1.5 billion people are said to depend on forests for their survival), the fight against corruption and organised crime. finally, illegal exploitation undermines the rule of law, good governance and respect for human rights.
in writing. europe has the highest proportion of older women in the world. these women are discriminated against in the labour market and their employment rate is much lower than that of men in the same age group. it is therefore necessary to ensure that discrimination against women over 50 is better taken into account and effectively combated. it is important to integrate gender equality in pension matters. it is also necessary to ensure that conditions are created which enable older women to remain in the labour market and/or to re-enter it. the violence against older women is also a phenomenon that is unfortunately still underestimated today. it is therefore imperative to combat all forms of violence. it would be a mistake to regard ageing as a negative factor affecting the social future of society. as long as the elderly retain a full place in society, they are certainly not a burden, as they can contribute to the general development, either as an actor or as a consumer.
in writing. on the eve of the european year of active ageing and solidarity between generations, the report adopted today highlights the often worrying situation of women nearing retirement. twenty-six per cent of women aged 55 and over are at risk of poverty, compared with 20.2 per cent of men. their careers are often interrupted by leave, part-time work or even maternity leave, and they often receive a pension that is less than that of men. this is why member states should effectively mainstream gender equality in the preparation and implementation of pension reforms. women over 55 also suffer from double discrimination in the labour market, which is why their employment rate is low. this trend must be counteracted and women must be allowed to remain in the labour market for as long as they wish.
in writing. - the logic behind the european commission's proposal for an effective eu strategy on raw materials has been reversed in mr bütikofer's report, and fortunately so. the ngos have been very critical. whereas the commission originally (and in that order) promoted access to raw materials on an international market, mining and then efficiency and recycling, the new report focuses primarily on efficiency, reuse, recycling and substitution of raw materials. the report is also strengthened by the fact that mining must not interfere with the eu's nature conservation objectives (natura 2000) and that it incorporates a new philosophy of cooperation with developing countries. it also contains a number of solutions for managing raw materials at european and international level. for example, supporting initiatives such as the extractive industries transparency initiative (eiti) increases transparency in accountability and responsibility. the social aspects of the raw materials problem are also taken into account. the report also condemns speculation in commodities. i am not sure that the wording is correct, but i do support this - i feel it is now - efficient eu strategy for raw materials.
in writing. everyone still remembers the oil spill caused by the deepwater horizon oil rig explosion in the gulf of mexico. the vote on this report was important as the european parliament is tackling the issue of securing these offshore oil and gas activities. emergency plans must be made available... and we also had to take a position in favour of extending the scope of the environmental liability directive so that the 'polluter pays' principle and strict liability apply to all damage to marine waters and biodiversity, so that oil and gas companies can be held responsible for any damage they may cause!
in writing. the deepwater horizon oil rig accident in the gulf of mexico in april 2010 reminded us of the dangers of offshore oil drilling to the environment, biodiversity and coastal communities. this is a reminder that the european parliament has taken note of, when it voted this afternoon on a resolution strengthening environmental and safety standards for all offshore oil and gas activities. this is an essential supply method since more than 90% of oil and 60% of gas in the eu is extracted from the sea. i am glad that the 'polluter pays' principle is clearly stated in the resolution. paragraph 76 explicitly calls for the scope of the environmental liability directive to be extended to all damage to marine waters and biodiversity, with increased liability for oil and gas companies which would assume full coverage of potential damage. the european parliament was also right to reject the proposal to introduce a moratorium on all new offshore oil drilling in eu waters: a choice disproportionate to the need to ensure high safety standards in european waters.
in writing. women entrepreneurship in small and medium-sized enterprises (smes) is a key issue. all studies show that the wealth generated by these companies contributes greatly to the economic growth of the european union. it is essential to support women who wish to start their own businesses, and support must be provided, but the situation must be reviewed in a global way, with tools that allow, in particular, to reconcile work and family life. i fully support this report, which offers some interesting ways of encouraging women to develop their businesses. raising awareness among young girls about entrepreneurship and management is essential if we are to try to reverse the prevailing trend. the european commission and the member states should set up programmes to this end. there is also a need to encourage networking among women entrepreneurs so that they can share their experiences and practices and highlight the obstacles they still face. the road ahead is long and deserves continuous attention!
in writing. removing obstacles to women's entrepreneurship in small and medium-sized enterprises is the whole point of the resolution voted on this afternoon by a large majority of the european parliament. the figures are alarming: in europe, one in four working men is an entrepreneur, while only one in ten women is an entrepreneur. the obstacles are well known: less social protection for the selfemployed, fewer rights, more risks and greater difficulties in reconciling work and private life. the member states have a good interest in exploring new ways of creating jobs: promoting women's entrepreneurship is part of this logic. for example, they would be well advised to promote under-exploited sources of finance, such as the progress microfinance programme, a european tool that allows people who want to start their own business but do not have access to traditional banking services to obtain loans of up to eur 25 000. our resolution also recalls the need to extend the 'erasmus for young entrepreneurs' programme, which allows them to work for six months with experienced entrepreneurs in another eu country: a real passport for the training of our young people and a worthwhile bet on the future.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this report on women entrepreneurship in smes. the latter, which account for 99% of european enterprises, provide two thirds of private sector jobs and generate more than half of the total value added created by enterprises active in the european union. however, too few women are still entrepreneurs: one in ten women is an entrepreneur, compared with one in four men. we must help them, at european and national level, to develop the full economic potential of smes. the development of women's networks is a major tool in this respect: i fully support the commission in its approach and hope that many women will choose to be part of the network of female entrepreneurship ambassadors.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as rapporteur for the flagship initiative on poverty reduction in the current context of budgetary pressure on the member states and the union, i am convinced that economic recovery in europe cannot be effective if we focus solely on budgetary austerity. the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy, in particular poverty reduction, are fundamental. social policies cannot be put on the back burner: they must be pursued in parallel with budgetary austerity. thus, in addition to ensuring a decent life for citizens, poverty reduction has significant economic consequences, such as supporting european consumption. homelessness is certainly one of the most advanced stages of homelessness for people in situations of poverty and social exclusion. once homeless, the reintegration into the labour market of the individual whose first concern is "where will i sleep tonight?" becomes even more difficult. i therefore support all the measures recommended in the oral question and the resolution, including the notion of affordable housing. in this respect, social housing is a matter for the member states, which are free to organise this service of general interest as they see fit. this element of the treaties must be recalled so that member states are never hindered in the fight against homelessness by rules on state aid. for all these reasons, we must support this resolution. i hope that it will be adopted by a large majority so that i can refer to it in my future report.
madam president, commissioner, i welcome this resolution on homelessness, because it is our responsibility to stress the extreme urgency of this. first of all, what was a priority yesterday remains an even more important priority today. the lack of a definition and reliable statistical indicators on homelessness does not prevent us from observing, with the help of the crisis, that the number of people living below the poverty line has increased, according to eurostat, from 79 million in 2009 to an estimated 84 million in 2011. ladies and gentlemen, three years ago, our parliament, in its concern to eradicate poverty, asked the member states to put an end to the problems of the homeless by 2015. today, are we any closer to that goal? has the year 2010 dedicated to the fight against poverty really been used by the member states to tackle this serious and permanent precariousness in a practical way? i have serious doubts about that and i regret it very much. in conclusion, i would like to stress the need to develop a comprehensive multi-sectoral strategy to deal with homelessness, because there is of course poverty and homelessness, but there are also family problems, health problems, various accidents and personal vulnerability. a comprehensive, effective, ambitious but tailor-made approach is needed, which takes account of individuals, their diverse backgrounds and their life circumstances. this is a basic right, at least, and many of the most deprived are deprived of it. on behalf of the alde group. – mr president, i think everybody here agrees that this is a very deep crisis, but we should not make the mistake at the beginning of this debate of saying that this is a greek debt crisis. the greek debt crisis is maybe the trigger, but what is really at stake is a deep crisis in the eurozone. first of all, we need to make an analysis of why we are in this crisis today, what went wrong. i think the reason is simple: first of all, we made a strategic mistake at the beginning when we launched the euro. we launched a monetary union, but we did not launch an economic and fiscal union, and we know that it is impossible to have one single currency with 17 different governments, 17 different bond markets, 17 different economic strategies. that does not exist anywhere in the world. why should it exist then in europe alone? i think we also made a mistake of method. what we have used over the last 10 years in europe is a bad method, a weak method, an intergovernmental method, and markets simply do not believe that member states can produce enough discipline and enough solidarity to keep together a single currency. that is what we in fact need. that is what markets are asking for. for the first time, we have markets which are not asking for more deregulation; no, they are they asking for more unity in europe, for a transfer of power to the european level. that is the request of the financial markets of today. to complete the analysis, i think that we have also had a bad attitude over the last 18 months, since the start of the crisis. we have seen political leadership in europe in the member states with a stop-and-go policy, a cacophony, half-measures and a lack of global approach. that global approach is what we need now, and what we need to hear from the european commission. what is the global approach that can stop the crisis and then recreate confidence in the markets? what do we need? i think we need four building blocks, and it is for the commission to come forward with these four building blocks. the first is a real economic governance and economic government. excuse me, but the proposals of mrs merkel and mr sarkozy a few weeks ago are not doing the job. a government of heads of state and government seeing each other twice a year is not a government. in my opinion, governments should see each other twice a week and not twice a year, as in the merkel/sarkozy proposal. the second building block is also very clear. we need a eurobond market, because the ecb cannot forever continue to buy bonds off countries in difficulties. that is not possible, so we need a eurobond market. what is the situation today in europe? the real situation in europe is that the bond market in europe is completely blocked. there are today no banks, insurance companies, pension funds or institutional investors who are still willing to buy bonds from a number of european countries and we are now dependent on savings from latin america and china to have enough liquidity in europe for the bonds of a number of european countries. that is the situation. so you have the choice. and in germany you have the choice – and the fdp has the choice, i shall be very blunt about this – either you continue with the situation where we are dependent on savings from outside europe or we create a european bond market now. and it is urgent to do it now and not to wait until the end of the year, as some are proposing. my third proposal, the third building block, is a growth and job act in europe. we need growth. let us do what the us government has done and announce a growth and job pact in europe. finally, mr president of the council, we need the stability pact, the 'six-pack'. let us be honest: yesterday we received a new proposal from your side and we are going backwards instead of forwards. i thought we had an agreement for real automaticity also in the preventive arm of the stability pact: that it is no longer the member states who have the lead, but it is the commission who has the lead. in the new proposal, last proposal i have seen, it is again the opposite. i say there is no deal if the member states do not understand that it is the commission which has to be in the lead of the stability pact and no longer the member states, as this no longer works in europe. my final message is clear: we want the commission to put a global proposal and a global approach on the table of parliament and the council. i can tell you, mr barroso: do that! it is the only way to put confidence back in the markets. that will be a huge global initiative by the commission, backed by the european parliament, and if you do that you can count on this european parliament.

mr president, millions of deaths could be avoided if member states tackled the risk factors for noncommunicable diseases more firmly. commissioner, that is the responsibility that we all have to bear, especially those taking part in the un high-level meeting. i would like to make three specific comments on the means of achieving this. first, the fight against overeating and poor nutrition must be a priority. our dietary habits, consisting of more refined foods, animal foods and fats, play a major role in the current epidemic of noncommunicable diseases. one study found that meat, dairy products, eggs and animal fats accounted for an average of 77 percent of saturated fatty acid intake and 100 percent of cholesterol intake in developed countries. it is therefore essential not to urge the maximum elimination of fatty acids, sugar, salt, for example, but to advocate moderation and responsible and balanced consumption, since only excessive consumption is harmful to health. secondly, alongside preventive and behavioural health policies, i would particularly like to stress the importance of the scientific contribution of research, which we must support to the maximum extent possible, including by devoting adequate financial resources to it. many treatments are still to be found, for example in the fight against cancer or alzheimer's disease, in comparison with which research on adult stem cells, for example, seems promising but unfortunately underfunded. finally, while the un general assembly offers the international community a unique opportunity to take action against noncommunicable diseases, it is essential that prevention efforts also find a home in families, schools, workplaces and businesses. a healthier lifestyle must be promoted everywhere and by all actors.
for the greens/efa group madam president, i will continue from where catherine trautmann left off. firstly, spectrum is - as mrs trautmann said - a rare commodity, and above all a common commodity, like so many other things: air, climate, water, etc. it must therefore be managed collectively and under the direction of the public authorities. in other words, no one can own all or part of the radio spectrum or consider himself to be so. secondly, if we accept that spectrum is a com mon good and a scarce good, we should exploit it in the most efficient and flexible way possible. so for us, the starting point is to first understand what the current use of spectrum is. that is why we insist on an inventory of spectrum allocation, because the allocation of frequencies is one thing and the use we make of them is another. if we allocate entire bands of spectrum to be used at 2 percent of their capacity, i don't consider that to be very efficient use. but if it is scarce, we should use it effectively and, of course, under the cover of a decision by the public authorities. finally, the radio spectrum is a public good that knows no borders. i would like to make the link here, as mr hökmark has done, with the whole debate on the future of european integration. we, the citizens of europe, are faced in each of our countries with the selfishness and the struggle for prerogatives of the member states, which say: 'don't touch, europe has nothing to do with this!' no, spectrum is a commodity without borders. for us europeans, it is obvious that the appropriate level to deal with the problem - even in a subsidiarity approach - is of course the european level. i think we all have to try to overcome national selfishness in our own countries. these are the three points i wanted to share with you in this debate.

in writing. two years after the global partnership on agriculture, food security and food was launched with great fanfare by the g8 heads of state at the l'aquila summit in 2009, the first results are still to come. the price of raw materials is skyrocketing, people in the horn of africa are starving, and the global financial crisis is taking away from us the basic right to food for all. the eu and the 27 member states remain, however, major political and financial actors, and the discussions on a new common food security policy are moving in the right direction. but is it up to the challenges of food security: unchecked population growth, pressures on natural resources and the adverse effects of climate change on agriculture? clearly, while it is important for the eu to provide a policy framework for the fight against world hunger, it is simply vital to make it a top priority. so that tomorrow, feeding all of humanity, with less water and land and three billion more people than the six of today, doesn't become an impossible task.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of the report by my colleague, gabriele zimmer, on a strategic framework of the european union to help developing countries to address food security challenges. the global food crisis, with nearly one billion people now facing it, is not only an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe but also a major threat to world peace and security. the urgency calls for the member states of the union to become immediately aware of the need to generate new investment in agriculture and rural development, to combat food speculation, to limit agrofuels, to ensure sufficient world stocks, to remove their own barriers to trade and to alleviate the debt of the countries most affected. according to projections, we should see an increase in the world's population, estimated at 9 billion people by 2050, with a 70% increase in food demand. to respond to this, land must be accessible to all, the land rights of small farmers must be protected in order to prevent a new agrarian colonialism, in particular through the land grabbing, which has become, in a few years, a scandalous reality.

are we able to stand united in this crisis? are we able to show real solidarity in this crisis, and have we the vision to do so, the courage to do so and the political leadership in the european union to do so? these are the questions that we need to face today. let us start with the state of the union. the state of the union is bad, but i think we have to face today’s reality. we are in the middle – not at the end – of a crisis, really in the centre of it. look at the reality. mistrust of banks has again risen over recent days and weeks. markets and stocks are at the lowest level since 2008. the international monetary fund yesterday lowered its growth forecast for europe for next year to only 1.1%, down from 1.6%. some economists are already talking about recession in the union. finally – this is important because we will come back to this later on – spreads: the tensions inside our markets have never been so high. before the financial crisis, the spreads in the eurozone – that is the difference between the average of the obligations, the bonds of other countries (and germany) – were only 19 – less than 20 – basic points. today the spreads are ten times higher. the average of the bonds in the eurozone – nt bonds – is more than 200 basic points, with, naturally, greece at 2 149 basic points of difference – a 21%-higher interest rate. in portugal there is a difference of more than 1 000, as there is in spain. in italy there is a difference of 400 basic points. these are tensions that are not sustainable. this must be solved not yesterday, not today but in a short time period because it is unsustainable to continue like this. there is a second question that we have to answer today. what solutions were provided for this crisis – mainly by the council, as has been indicated, and mainly by the member states? because it needs unanimity; the polish know about that, as poland disappeared in the 18th century because of the unanimity rule in the polish parliament: that is history and reality. the same could happen in europe if we continue with this unanimity rule. we have to abolish it. colleagues, this is the real problem. why is there such a problem in this crisis? in writing. i voted for the excellent report by my colleague sylvie goulard on budgetary surveillance in the euro area. it is a key component of the legislative package on economic governance reform, known in european parlance as the 'six pack'. the report's strong proposal is: 'member states whose currency is the euro should pool [...] per cent of sovereign debt in the form of solidarity commitments (euro area securities). " this is the idea that european liberals have been pushing for months, calling for the creation of eurobonds, i.e. debt mutualisation and the ability for countries currently in austerity to borrow at reasonable rates on the markets. of course, sharing debts does not make them go away. it goes without saying that greece, like other countries at risk, must first commit to a clean-up of its public finances. but the greatest strength of eurobonds, beyond the reduction in the financial costs borne by the member states, is certainly the promotion of the euro as a safe-haven currency. a credible alternative to the dollar, as 25% of china's foreign exchange reserves are already held in the european currency.
in writing. today, defending the european union means calling for more economic and budgetary governance and advocating the sacred union. the haglund report, which was adopted this afternoon by 395 votes to 64 with 201 abstentions, mainly from left-wing parties, shows the latter's aversion to discipline and sanctions, since that is what this regulation is all about, which aims to provide solutions to the excessive macroeconomic imbalances in the euro zone! the european parliament has wisely decided to provide for flexible sanctions in the event of non-compliance by member states with the recommendations of the commission and the council on the major economic aggregates, which are mainly income, investment, consumption, the unemployment rate and inflation. for my part, i welcome this far-reaching reform of the governance framework based on the community method, which goes far beyond the traditional budgetary surveillance and ensures greater independence for the commission in monitoring the economic policies of the member states. only the coherence of the 27 macroeconomic policies and the reduction of fiscal and social competition will enable the european union to return to the path of sustainable growth and jobs.
in writing. i welcome the adoption this afternoon of the report on the economic governance package, now known as the 'six pack' in european parlance. a decisive vote and a step forward towards european economic governance, towards a more federal europe too. this package of measures will not save the euro from the current difficulties. but these structural measures are drawing lessons from the current crisis and from the lax fiscal policies of the past 20 years. the ford report on strengthening the budgetary frameworks of the member states helps to set the bar and draws particular lessons from the greek case. in essence, it consists in imposing more stringent and binding rules on the member states in the preparation of their national budgets. it also imposes the independence of national statistical institutes and provides for penalties in the event of falsification of figures transmitted to the european institutions, an imperative necessity, given the extent to which greece tampered with its statistics at the time of its accession to the euro area in 2001.

in writing. at present, people with disabilities represent about 15% of the european population, or between 80 and 120 billion people. this means the enormous potential of a workforce that wants to be seen as part of the vital forces of their country. the number is not likely to decrease with the increase in life span and the advances in medicine. one of the five main objectives of the europe 2020 strategy is to increase the employment rate of the population aged 20-64 from 69% to no more than 75% by 2020. to achieve this, the integration of disabled people into the world of work is necessary. the adoption of a first european directive requiring employers to make 'reasonable accommodation' is evidence that european intervention can be useful, especially in countries where disability is not yet well taken into account. the inclusion of people with disabilities also requires the recognition of sign language as an official language. europe must set an example in the field of the employment of people with disabilities. it must help to combat the prejudices which hold back business leaders and encourage headhunters to "dare" to hire. it is a sign of openness and respect for universal values.
in writing. taking into account only the consequences of the ageing population of european countries, the number of people who are "addicted" is likely to double by 2050, according to eurostat forecasts. the kosa report voted on this afternoon therefore stresses the need to improve the living conditions of disabled people. it is first and foremost a question of human rights, of respect for people who are doubly disadvantaged, first by their disability and secondly by the too many daily obstacles they face. more vulnerable, disabled people face physical difficulties (limited access to goods and services, public transport, etc.) but also social difficulties (few employment opportunities, limited access to means of communication, etc.). the adoption of this report makes it possible to establish a number of objectives to be achieved by the member states in terms of equal opportunities, such as increasing the employment rate of disabled people, their mobility and their participation in public life. the creation of a european mobility card aimed at harmonising care for disabled people or access to services and means of communication for visually or hearing impaired people would be valuable steps in this direction.
in writing. - the mobility of workers is one of the pillars of european policy, with the need to remove obstacles of an administrative nature in particular. the aim of increased mobility is also to lead to the recognition of qualifications and, in particular, to the progressive harmonization of social and wage conditions. the latter has not yet been achieved, and particular attention must be paid to preventing mobility from being turned into its opposite, social dumping, whereby low-wage countries are used to undermine existing social and collective agreements.
in writing. the free movement of people and workers has become one of the symbols of european integration and is regarded by europeans as the most positive result of this integration. however, too few people exercise this right. despite the initiatives taken to promote the mobility of workers, too many barriers of a social, linguistic, cultural, legal and administrative nature still remain. the member states must play a key role in promoting the exercise of this right. there is thus a need for greater cooperation to remove obstacles to moving to find a job. smes are a major source of job creation and can provide a real impetus to economic recovery and development. it is therefore essential to support them and involve them in the process. better mobility allows for an exchange of experience which benefits both employers and employees, and the objective of job creation will be more easily achieved if labour mobility is fully realised. priority should also be given to investment in vocational education and training and to the exchange of professional experience.

in writing. the economic and financial crisis has shown the limits of global governance as it exists. our economic management must be based on an approach that focuses on traditional macroeconomic and financial policies on the one hand and on a policy that gives priority to job creation and social protection on the other, because without a take-off in domestic demand there can be no sustainable recovery. it should be borne in mind that during the crisis, the world economy lost about 30 million jobs. europe needs comprehensive and joint solutions to overcome the persistent problems of the financial sector and sovereign debts. cooperation is essential to the stability of the world economy and must take precedence over national interests. it is therefore essential that the international institutions which are the focus of this cooperation reflect the changes of the last quarter of a century.

in writing. the concept of the family unit is evolving to reflect changes in our societies. single mothers represent 5% of european women, and 85% of these mothers are aged 25-64. these women, who are often in a vulnerable situation, must be given special attention by our governments, since they share the challenges faced by all two-parent families, such as education, training, employment, etc. this accumulation of difficulties has repercussions for the children. the latter must have the same opportunities in education and access to the labour market as children from two-parent families. it is up to the eu, which is concerned to uphold the values of equality, democracy and freedom, to raise awareness among those member states which have not yet adapted their economic and social policies to these new family models. the single mother and the single father are still discriminated against in some eu countries and regions. the right to be different is a fundamental expression of human rights. every minority, whatever the nature of what makes it a minority, must enjoy the same rights.
in writing. the adoption this afternoon of barbara matera's report on the situation of single mothers marks a step forward in improving the status of these single women in relation to responsibilities usually borne by couples. it is essential that member states pay particular attention to single-parent families, which are more vulnerable financially, discriminated against in the labour market and victims of social prejudice. less flexible working hours, particular exposure to stress, social exclusion, lack of flexible training, etc. are all obstacles that single mothers, representing about 85% of single-parent families, see adding to the already existing inequalities between men and women. these families have specific needs. it is necessary to provide concrete responses and to adapt the policies of the member states. tax credits, health care subsidies, tax breaks, incentives for businesses that offer childcare facilities and day care, flexible employment opportunities, training available to single mothers, etc. there are many measures that could help to reduce the inequalities suffered by these women. not to mention better sex education for teenagers, which is essential to combat the increase in single-parent families.

member of the commission. − mr president, the commission expresses its concern regarding the social and economic consequences that the closure of arcelormittal and nokia will bring. some 600 direct job losses, as well as indirect job losses at suppliers, are concerned. in the case of nokia, at least 3 000 jobs may be affected. a company’s decision to close down production plants is for the company itself to make. however, the european union can play a role, and the company needs to follow specific rules. as a very minimum, the commission expects arcelormittal and nokia to observe strictly the eu directives on information and consultation, collective redundancies and european works councils. the commission also expects arcelormittal to comply with the agreements it concluded and the commitments it entered into with employees and local authorities. the eu can also provide specific support. the european social fund offers re-training of workers, including various forms of assistance such as counselling, help towards self-employment, and so on. if it is not possible to keep the jobs, and the workers are made redundant, belgium or romania, in this case, could apply for support from the european globalisation adjustment fund (egf) if the fund’s criteria are met. first contacts between the belgian and romanian authorities and the egf services of the commission have already been made. more generally, i would like to highlight the main challenges that we face. first, it is becoming increasingly clear that growth is at risk in the eu. indeed, recent projections showed that growth in many countries across the globe – especially in developed countries – is strongly decelerating. the eu economy is no exception to this trend. the sovereign debt crisis is making things even worse for several euro area countries by pushing up interest rates and further affecting confidence. second, employment is a major concern. in the second quarter of 2011, employment growth measured over four quarters was a meagre 0.3%, and in august the eu unemployment rate was still stuck at 9.5%, the same level as at the start of the year. in contrast to our assessment in the spring, when the prospect was one of job-loss recovery, we now have to fear an employment crisis in the eu with a number of negative features: high youth unemployment, which is twice as high as the average unemployment rates; high structural unemployment with high budgetary and human costs; long-term unemployment, which has already risen from its earlier level of under 3% of the active population pre-crisis to just over 4% in the middle of this year; and rising levels of precariousness. the recent recovery in employment stems mainly from an increase in temporary jobs, as the number of workers on a permanent contract has risen only moderately over the past four quarters. finally, there is increasing social unrest as a result of the deterioration in employment, the implementation of severe austerity measures and wage cuts in the context of persisting inequality. indeed, there is an increasing perception among europeans that the cost of the crisis is not equally shared, with the poor suffering the most – and, as we have seen, this is a potentially explosive situation. in the short term, it is important that eu policymakers provide a clear, coherent and comprehensive response in order to calm financial markets and bring back confidence. this plan should address structural flaws in the economic and monetary union and concerns about greece and other countries, but should also revive the growth potential of the individual member states. the state of our public finances is very weak and we face lower growth expectations in the near future. this means that labour market recovery cannot rely on public stimulus measures and it cannot rely on gdp growth pulling the huge numbers of jobseekers back into the labour market. what we need to do is improve the functioning of europe’s labour markets. existing labour supply and labour demand will need to come together sooner; job matching should be more efficient; and existing jobs will need to last longer and be more productive. with precisely this in mind, the commission issued country-specific recommendations just before the summer break. these recommendations provide specific guidance on labour market functioning, tailored to each member state’s situation and covering a wide range of labour market reforms including payroll taxes, childcare, education systems, wage-setting mechanisms and retirement patterns. having said all this, of course, what matters is not just what we say in brussels: at the end of the day, what matters is what the member states do, what governments do and what firms do. in order to be successful in improving labour markets, we need to build, and to make use of, the right partnerships in member states, with the social partners and the private sector. the commission has proposed a roadmap for stability and growth to resolve the current crisis. furthermore, our next annual growth survey will present further proposals focusing on how to promote a growth-enhancing agenda that helps to create and maintain jobs in europe. in spite of extremely adverse market and financial situations, companies and their workforces throughout europe have, by and large, engaged creatively in restructuring processes that were constructive, effective and instrumental in limiting job losses. the commission wants to encourage permanent business adaptation to swiftly changing economic circumstances while maintaining a high degree of employment and social protection. measures supporting the reallocation of resources across firms and sectors are strongly needed. they include employment protection legislation and business practices related to corporate restructuring which do not hinder the reallocation of resources, across sectors, towards higher-value-added and faster-growth activities. in recent years, the eu has put a substantial amount of energy and effort into promoting adaptation to change and restructuring. as announced in the communication on ‘industrial policy’, in the single market act and in the ‘new skills and jobs’ flagship initiative, the commission wishes to put adaptation to change and restructuring on the agenda of public authorities, the social partners and other concerned stakeholders by means of a new consultation exercise. its objective will be to disseminate and apply the good practice across europe in the field of anticipation, preparation and socially responsible management of restructuring. the commission will be using the knowledge and experience acquired over the past few years, including through the restructuring forums, studies and seminars. however, we must recognise that this acquis is still largely unknown to economic and social players. furthermore, the commission considers that it needs to be reviewed in the light of the economic crisis. the egf currently works with two possible intervention criteria: an application can be made either on trade-related grounds or on the basis of the global financial and economic crisis. this second criterion is time limited and runs out for applications presented after the end of 2011. as the unemployment situation in the eu is still far from recovering, the commission has proposed – with the clear support of parliament but without, so far, having achieved a qualified majority in the council – an extension of this so-called ‘crisis’ derogation. the commission is doing all it can to ensure that the crisis remains an intervention criterion for the egf after the end of the current year and until the end of 2013, when the new egf regulation, proposed as part of the cohesion package on 6 october 2011, should enter into effect.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as my colleague mr cramer has pointed out, competition is only meaningful if it is competition in relation to the road. that's where we need to gain market share. i am glad that the difficult debate on the complete separation of infrastructure and operation has been postponed, especially since - at any rate in my country, a small country with a very dense network - too much separation has led to a great deal of disorganization, a great deal of additional costs, without any new benefits, or new entrants. then what's the point? there's not really enough new entrants. secondly, i think that what we need is obviously a strong and independent regulator. we need separation but also essential functions. let us look at it function by function and not ideologically, to see which functions are those on which, indeed, separation is needed. when we go so far as to say that we want to separate it or human resources, i don't see very well what that can do in terms of economies of scale. thirdly, on rail services, i think i tabled an amendment with my colleague mr cramer to article 13. if a workshop does not have the residual capacity to accommodate a new demand, why do we want to force it to do so, if not to disorganize the work it already provides or the service it already provides? so i think an interesting job has been done. there is a big one ahead of us and here are a few points on which i think we could still improve the text a little.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i would first of all like to thank all those who have participated in a constructive spirit in the preparation of this report: my colleagues, representative associations and also collaborators. in 2010, 116 million people were at risk of poverty, i.e. more than 20% of our citizens and 8% of europeans were living in extreme material deprivation, certainly more today with the crises we are experiencing. the 2020 strategy adopted here set itself the goal of reducing the number of poor by 20 million and this platform aims to be the tool of this fight against this phenomenon, which in itself represents a violation of basic human rights. the report therefore aims, beyond specifying the method of its operation, above all to give the union and the member states a roadmap with recommendations for policies to be implemented to achieve this objective. the adoption of this resolution by this parliament is therefore of particular importance in the current political and economic context. citizens must see that the union is concerned not only with the debt of the member states but also with their economic and social situation and that there are still european institutions and elected representatives who promote solidarity between states and between citizens. a word about current affairs and the food aid programme for the poorest of the poor which we want to keep at 500 million in the short and long term; it's in the report. the council of agriculture ministers yesterday reached agreement to do so, at least in the short term. that's good! this is a positive sign. that was the least of it, but what worries me is the reluctance, or even the threats, of some member states against the union's social policies before they get there. and the long-term problem is not yet solved. the following are some of the other key points raised in this report. first, several categories of people who are more vulnerable to poverty risk such as children, women, the elderly, the disabled, migrants or roma require a specific approach and are therefore treated separately in the report. then there are various factors that can lead to poverty. they are also the subject of special recommendations. this is the case, for example, with the shortage of decent and affordable housing, decent jobs, quality and accessible social services without discrimination, education systems that avoid school drop-out or vocational training adapted to the labour market or, simply, financial resources to meet basic needs, hence the need for a minimum income in europe under community legislation. in order to carry out these actions at european level, we are naturally asking the commission to mobilise european funds to finance initiatives to combat poverty, in particular the european social fund or the european globalisation adjustment fund. one thing must be clear: public policy cannot be pursued at european level, as at national level, without adequate funding. social investment to fight poverty and thus boost job-creating growth and thus start a virtuous circle is therefore essential. i would like to emphasize one point. austerity measures in the framework of european economic governance must not jeopardise employment or social protection. it is not enough to monitor the inflation, deficit and debt curve. the member states must also be accountable for the development of poverty and parliament will have to be regularly informed. the report therefore stresses the need for regular monitoring of member states' progress within the platform. all these recommendations were widely discussed at the first convention of the platform in krakow and were received quite favourably by the actors on the ground in the fight against poverty, whose involvement is fundamental, as the report recommends. i therefore call on my colleagues to give massive support to this report, as was done in committee, so that this parliament can finally give the citizens a positive signal in these times of suffering.
mr president, there is one aspect of the problem of poverty and social exclusion which has not been discussed in this debate, and that is the fact that the member states of the european union import poverty and social exclusion on a large scale. every year hundreds of thousands, if not more, of immigrants from outside the european union arrive. many of these people are integrated into the social security system of the member state in which they are established. people without job prospects, people without integration opportunities, people with very high language backlogs from the start. i think it is very important that the member states change course and adopt a policy of non-discrimination towards potential immigrants coming to europe who have no prospect of work or integration. this massive import of poverty must be stopped as soon as possible, because the absorption capacity of the member states has already been far exceeded. the report under discussion rightly points to the problem of many immigrants from outside the eu ending up in poverty. but to tackle this problem it is important that a restrictive immigration policy is pursued, that there is also another way of investing in the countries of origin of these immigrants, so that the money is no longer wasted but that the money is used to create jobs there.
member of the commission. − madam president, i agree with everyone who spoke in the discussion in the spirit of reinforcing our efforts to combat poverty and social exclusion in europe, at eu level and also in the member states. i agree with what was emphasised in the discussion: that the centrality of employment policies – the availability and the quality of jobs – is highly important, and therefore employment policies have to play a stronger role. wherever possible, job creation has to be front-loaded and cannot just wait until economic growth and recovery creates jobs again at some point. in programme countries, but also in countries where there is greater room for manoeuvre for the government through targeted interventions and initiatives, i believe it is possible to create jobs and reverse the negative trends. there is a great role – and this is what we also stressed at the european platform meeting in krakow – for social innovation. perhaps more could have been said about this in today’s discussion. however, we believe that this is going to be an effective tool for finding and disseminating new and effective solutions to poverty. in particular, for example, the situation of minorities and other marginalised and disadvantaged groups, or new areas like digital inclusion should be explored in this way. that is why it is also very important that, in addition to the esf and other well-known financial instruments, there will be a new eu-level facility for supporting social innovation. more solidarity is needed in the eu but also within the member states. i believe that, although we are in quite a late and very dangerous phase of the financial crisis, this is now being increasingly recognised. in certain member states there are new directions concerning, for example, the role of taxation in fiscal consolidation or the new negotiations on a minimum wage in germany, which i very strongly welcome. this connects with the call which i heard from many participants in the debate about further legislative proposals in this area. i believe legislative proposals should not be ruled out, but they only make sense if they have a chance of being passed and implemented. so we have to continue to look at what is really causing the problem here, and how this should be addressed. i believe that if we look into the question of how we have arrived at this point, with a huge number and an increasing proportion of badly-paid jobs, we should pay attention to a trend which is a polarisation of the wage structure in europe, particularly as a consequence of the large-scale loss of industrial jobs in the recent past, which was aggravated by the financial and economic crisis. that resulted in the disappearance of many medium-paid jobs, the so-called ‘hollowing out’ effect in the labour market. that, i believe, requires primarily a stronger employment dimension to industrial policies, which is why we have to reinforce industrial policies at eu level and make a stronger connection between job creation and the sustainability of jobs and industrial policy. i agree with those who stressed or hinted that, if macroeconomic policies are half-baked, social policies have a very difficult starting point. this is why it is very important that there is better coherence between all these policies, which is what we would like to achieve in the next european semester. finally, i will mention one issue which many members of the house spoke about: food aid for the deprived. the commission was, from the very outset, determined to address the legal problem and begin discussions in council in order to secure the provision of similar quantities of foodstuffs for the next two years. on 3 october, i presented an amended proposal for the pending regulation extending the legal basis to the relevant chapter of the treaty, i.e. social cohesion. i am extremely happy that the member states reached a compromise yesterday in the council. the commission services will now make the necessary changes in order to ensure the continuation of this scheme.
the rapporteur. - madam president, at the end of this debate, i am pleased to see the broad support of most of my colleagues this morning - and i thank them for this report, for this road map, which is multifaceted and contains complementary recommendations, and i believe that this is important. perhaps a word about the minimum income which still elicits reactions sometimes based on misunderstandings. in fact, in our report we have drawn up a compromise on this important subject which takes account of the specific features and living standards of each state and which, mrs lynne, is in the nuanced sense that you have expressed. i think it's a really useful tool, but with the nuances that it has to have. i also welcome the statements and intentions of our commissioner andor, which are in line with the wishes of parliament, particularly in the areas of employment, child poverty, gender equality, access to social services and, above all, the refinancing of social cohesion funds. mr andor, we must ensure that these intentions, your initiatives and your concrete proposals for 2012 can be put into practice. as you said, the european parliament, together with the commission, must put pressure on the member states to make solidarity between citizens a reality, a priority in the union, especially in the context of the crisis we are experiencing. the more united parliament is in this struggle, the stronger our signal will be.
the european platform against poverty and social exclusion is one of the flagships of the eu 2020 strategy. the fight against poverty is rightly highlighted as a major priority and challenge for the eu: it's our ambition to lift 20 million people out of poverty by 2020. over the past 10 years, the poverty rate in the eu has increased or, at best, remained constant. in most countries, the lowest benefits and the last safety net, the living wage or minimum income, fell. we cannot and must not accept this: families can't make ends meet and live in poverty. i hope that the european platform against poverty and social exclusion will provide a good basis for our joint fight against poverty in the eu. finally, i would like to refer to the european food programme for the least privileged. yesterday a political agreement was reached for the years 2012 and 2013. i think this is an important signal: the programme is indispensable for the approximately 18 million europeans it supports each year. but we can 't leave it at this . we must also seek to ensure adequate funding for the period after 2013 so that the programme can continue.
